title: Shadow traffic before you ship a prompt change
excerpt: Unit tests on golden prompts miss the weird traffic that shows up on Monday morning. Here is how I shadow new prompts and models against live traffic without users eating the regressions.
content:
You can pass every offline eval and still break checkout copy, support tone, or tool-calling rates the day a new system prompt hits production. Offline sets are curated. Production is not.

Shadow traffic is the bridge: run the candidate config on real requests, score it offline, promote only if it wins — users never see the experiment until it earns the cutover.

---

## What "shadow" means here

For a sample of production requests:

1. Serve the **current** prompt/model to the user (unchanged).
2. Asynchronously run the **candidate** on the same input.
3. Log both outputs with the same `request_id`.
4. Score later — automated metrics + sampled human review.
5. Promote only when the candidate clears your bars.

The user experience stays stable. Your confidence does not depend on hope.

---

## 1. Sample on purpose

You do not need 100% duplication on day one.

- Start at 1–5% of traffic, stratified by route or intent if you can
- Cap concurrency and budget so shadowing cannot DDOS your provider bill
- Exclude requests with known secrets or regulated payloads if logging full text is restricted — shadow metadata-only or redacted inputs instead

Shadowing is an experiment harness, not a second production.

---

## 2. Score what users would feel

Benchmark MMLU will not tell you if the new prompt stopped calling `create_refund` correctly.

I track, per variant:

| Signal | Why |
|--------|-----|
| Task success / tool schema validity | Did it do the job? |
| Groundedness / citation checks (RAG) | Did it invent? |
| Safety / refusal agreement with policy | Did guardrails drift? |
| Latency and tokens | Hidden cost regressions |
| Pairwise preference on a sample | Tone and clarity |

Automate what you can. Human-review a fixed weekly sample — especially disagreements between control and candidate.

---

## 3. Keep identity and side effects out of the shadow path

The shadow run must not:

- Send email, charge cards, or write to prod databases
- Use write-capable tools — stub them or use a dry-run mode
- Share rate limits so aggressively that prod throttles

Read-only tools can be shared carefully. Mutation tools get fakes that return realistic payloads for scoring.

---

## 4. Promote with a gate, not a vibe

Define the bar before the experiment:

- No statistically meaningful drop on critical intents
- Safety metrics non-worse
- Cost within +X%
- Latency within +Y ms at p95

If the candidate wins on tone but loses on tool validity, it does not ship. Write that down so Friday-afternoon pressure cannot redefine "good."

---

## 5. Wire it into the same deploy path as code

Prompt changes should go through the same review and rollback story as application code:

- Versioned prompt config in git
- Shadow job as a required check for risky changes
- One-click rollback to the previous version id

If prompt deploys are a console paste, shadow traffic will not save you — process will.

---

Offline evals catch the bugs you already thought of. Shadow traffic catches the ones your users invent. Run both. Ship the candidate only when live traffic says it is ready — not when the PR description does.
